Context/Background:
Intraductal papillary neoplasms (IPNs),  including intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), intraductal oncocytic papillary neoplasms (IOPNs), and intraductal tubulopapillary neoplasms (ITPNs), are clinically detectable macroscopic non-invasive cyst-forming lesions, some of which progress to invasive pancreatic cancer. Proteins and glycoproteins have proven to be useful clinical biomarkers for classifying cyst-forming neoplasms in the pancreas.Here, we used proteomics and glycoproteomics to characterize a series of histologically and genetically well-characterized surgically resected IPNs, including IPMNs and IOPNs.

Our analysis included 69 IPNs (64 IPMNs and 5 IOPNs), 76 macro-dissected grossly normal duct tissues (NDs, with 32 of the 76 NDs coming from the same resection specimens as the IPNs), and 32 cyst fluid samples (22 from matched IPMN patients, 3 matched IOPN patients, 2 from unrelated IPMN patients, and 5 other cysts).
Prompt: Look at the differential genes between IPMN and ND samples, provide a summary of enriched pathways in IPMN compared to ND.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
Samples: Surgically resected pancreatic intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs, n = 64) versus grossly normal duct (ND, n = 76) proteomes. Assay: quantitative proteomics/glycoproteomics (Table S2A). Contrast: IPMN vs. ND. No raw counts; input was per‐protein log₂FC and FDR.  

Keywords  
• Mucin biology (mucins)  
• Translation/ribosome  
• Immune response  
• Epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT)  
• Glycosylation  

Candidate Genes  
MUC1, MUC5AC, QSOX1, RPLP1, FN1, NFKB1  

Pathway Enrichments

| KRAS Signaling Dn         | Down      | RSAD2, HNF1A, TENT5C, GAMT, CALML5, GP2, GTF3C5, NOS1, UGT2B17  |

Analysis  
IPMNs show pronounced suppression of core protein‐synthesis machinery (ribosome, translation initiation, peptide biosynthesis and pancreatic‐secretion modules; 56% of KEGG, 42% of Reactome, 31% of GO terms down) alongside activation of immune/inflammatory and stromal remodeling programs (Salmonella-infection/phagosome, interferon-gamma, complement, EMT, integrin signaling; 44–80% of pathways up). The hallmarks of EMT and IFN-γ response (FDR < 0.05) suggest early fibrotic/stromal alterations and immune engagement in non-invasive IPMN epithelium.  

Targeted Keyword-Guided Subset  
– “Mucin”: MUC1 and MUC5AC are significantly up in IPMN (log₂FC 0.64 and 2.99; FDR < 1e-4) but no mucin‐specific pathway term appeared, indicating mucin overexpression as a standalone marker rather than pathway driver.  
– “Translation”: Strong downregulation of cytoplasmic translation and ribosome‐related terms.  
– “Immune response”: Enrichment of interferon-gamma, complement, phagosome pathways.  
– “EMT”: Enriched in Hallmark EMT (NES 3.28, FDR 0.026).  
– “Glycosylation”: No glycosylation‐specific GO or Reactome term passed FDR < 0.05; QSOX1 (glycoprotein maturase) is upregulated though.  

Key Genes/Proteins (Leading Edge)  

Up in IPMN  
| Gene   | Direction | Role/Function                         | Pathway(s)                           |
|--------|-----------|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| FN1    | Up        | ECM glycoprotein, cell adhesion       | Hallmark EMT; Integrin signaling    |
| NFKB1  | Up        | Transcription factor, immune signaling| Salmonella infection; IFNγ response  |
| QSOX1  | Up        | Flavin‐dependent sulfhydryl oxidase   | Glycoprotein secretion (by function) |
| MUC5AC | Up        | Secreted mucin                        | –                                    |

Down in IPMN  
| Gene   | Direction | Role/Function                         | Pathway(s)                          |
|--------|-----------|---------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
| RPLP1  | Down      | Ribosomal P protein, translation      | Ribosome; Cytoplasmic translation   |
| RPS14  | Down      | Ribosomal S protein, translation      | Translation initiation; peptide biosynthesis |

Comparisons & Confidence  
The concordant suppression of multiple translation‐related modules across KEGG and Reactome underscores a IPMN‐specific reduction in protein‐synthesis capacity. Immune and EMT signals are robust across Hallmark and KEGG (FDR < 0.05), suggesting genuine stromal/immune engagement. Mucin overexpression (MUC1/5AC) is a strong single‐protein signal but without dedicated pathway enrichment.

Implications & Next Steps  
1. Validate suppression of translation machinery (e.g., polysome profiling) in IPMN epithelium.  
2. Investigate fibrotic/EMT programs via immunohistochemistry for FN1 and mesenchymal markers.  
3. Examine QSOX1’s role in glycoprotein maturation and cyst fluid biomarker potential.  
4. Explore immune cell infiltration and IFN-γ signaling in IPMN microenvironment (flow cytometry/IHC).
